title: Sources: an unusually high volume of Nvidia GPUs, including thousands of B300s, hit the market after the US curbed Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips
excerpt: Sources: an unusually high volume of Nvidia GPUs, including thousands of B300s, hit the market after the US curbed Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips
title_en: Sources: an unusually high volume of Nvidia GPUs, including thousands of B300s, hit the market after the US curbed Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips
excerpt_en: Sources: an unusually high volume of Nvidia GPUs, including thousands of B300s, hit the market after the US curbed Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips
content_en:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.

Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.

Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.

The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.

The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.

Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.

Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

## Scrutiny over Chinese access to Nvidia chips

Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.

The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI, of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."

"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.

"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."

During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

title: Every, a media company that provides consulting services to help companies become AI-native, raised a $17.5M Series A at a $110M post-money valuation
excerpt: Every, a media company that provides consulting services to help companies become AI-native, raised a $17.5M Series A at a $110M post-money valuation
title_en: Every, a media company that provides consulting services to help companies become AI-native, raised a $17.5M Series A at a $110M post-money valuation
excerpt_en: Every, a media company that provides consulting services to help companies become AI-native, raised a $17.5M Series A at a $110M post-money valuation
content_en:
Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.

Shipper’s right: VC-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. But Shipper is betting that Every—currently with about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid—can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game.

Hence, the fundraise: Every recently raised $17.5 million in Series A funding, at a $110 million post-money valuation, *Fortune* has exclusively learned. IA Ventures’s Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company, and is changing his title to “Philosopher King,” which I rib him about. He good-naturedly says the change is semiotic.

“The really important thing about taking the money for me was that we’d do it in a way that allows us to achieve our goals… and do it in a way that doesn’t require us to sacrifice our soul or the things about the company that I love deeply,” said Shipper. “I think of changing my title as a symbolic thing. If this was a normal venture capital deal, that would be completely off the table and ridiculous.”

And this isn’t a normal venture deal, in a couple of ways. First, Every is a media company. With its neoclassical pop art aesthetic, Every has a multi-pronged business model: Its writing serves a professional audience seeking to become “AI-native,” while the 35-person company also provides consulting services to large companies and produces conferences (I recently interviewed Shipper at Every’s Thesis: 2027 conference in Brooklyn). Second, Shipper didn’t raise in a standard startup process: IA’s Beyroutey and Shipper are close friends (they went to college together) and Shipper went straight to Beyroutey.

“I didn’t shop the deal,” said Shipper. “I went to someone I deeply trust, who understands the business deeply, who understands exactly what I want to do with it, and has put me in the position where I make all the decisions to build the company in the way that I want to build it,” Shipper said. “I think that’s the only way to build a business like this, because this is a very unique shape. It’s a media company and a technology company, kind of smushed together.”

Shipper started Every in 2020, about six years after exiting his first startup, co-browsing company Firefly, in 2014 (the acquisition came right as he was graduating college). He spent the intervening years finding the right next thing. Every became the answer, in part because it addressed a number of questions that Shipper had been asking throughout his life. For one, he’d long felt tension between writing and entrepreneurship (at Every he could be both). He’d also been interested in tech since he was a kid.

“I thought a lot about why Microsoft and Windows had worked, and one of the big reasons is that they came during a hardware platform shift, from mainframes to PCs,” said Shipper. “They started building operating systems for that, and that’s always a really big opportunity…. And I thought: I wonder what my platform shift is going to be?”

Shipper and Every are all-in on AI, and the company is built to help people understand how they can actually use AI, in their jobs and their lives.

“I think too few companies are trying to do that,” said Shipper. “Too many companies are trying to build the machine god or are worrying about Armageddon, and I’m not…. I would expect improvements we’re seeing \[in AI\] to continue, and I would expect there to be a gap between the improvements that you see on the charts and how well those improvements translate into actually better work by people (and that people at companies are proud of). Our job is to fill that gap.”

Shipper is optimistic that AI won’t replace humans at work, a common fear and feature of AI discourse.

“The narrative is ‘it’s so over for humans’, and I think that’s exactly wrong,” he said. “That relies on this sleight of hand where you forget that humans are the ones who make these things, and humans are the ones that prompt these things—and decide what’s valuable and what’s not.”

In some sense, Shipper expects AI to eventually blur into the background, much in the same way we don’t really say “I used the Internet.”

“Ultimately, I think the technology and the model advances will disappear, and we’ll actually just think about the humans that did it,” said Shipper. “Asking if Claude did it will be like asking if you used your laptop. ‘Did your laptop do it?’ No, you did it.”

Happy Thanksgiving and we’ll see you again on Monday.

**Allie Garfinkle X:** @agarfinks

content_en:
### Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

### Model overkill

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

### Cost concerns

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”

### Hidden expenses

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

- AT&T Corp. shifted 40% of its AI workloads to open models and plans to grow that share to 70%, according to The Information. By delegating tasks such as code summarization to cheaper engines and using a router to direct work to the most efficient model, the telecom giant cut AI operating costs by 56% with only a 2% decline in quality.
- Pinterest Inc. achieved over 90% cost savings on its AI operations by moving away from frontier models, said William Ready said on the company’s second fiscal quarter earnings call in August.
- Uber Technologies Inc., which unexpectedly burned through an entire year’s AI budget in the first four months of this year, has cut model requests by one-third and costs per session by over half since February, largely by shifting more workloads to open-weight models.

title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"
excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back on an Axios report saying some employees believe humanity will hand power to superintelligent systems. title_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"
excerpt_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back on an Axios report saying some employees believe humanity will hand power to superintelligent systems. Amodei says "turning over governance to AI is a bad idea." The article Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea" appeared first on The Decoder .
content_en:
# Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"

**Dario Amodei said it was "absurd" to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will" to AI systems.**

In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions. The outlet reported that some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems, and often should, rather than fight for control.

AI must be governed by "legitimate democratic processes," Amodei wrote. Political decisions should stay in human hands, he argued, and he rejected handing power to AI as firmly as he rejected autocracy.

> \[...\] We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination on the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word to governance by AI, and I feel just as strongly that handing over governance to AI is a bad idea.
>
> Dario Amodei

Automating specific tasks such as driving, developing cancer drugs, and writing software could benefit humanity, Amodei said, but that was a different matter from giving up free will in politics.

## Amodei says that full automation isn't always worth the risk

End-to-end automation could also bring risks, Amodei wrote, including serious job disruption and AI building new models without human oversight. "It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives," he wrote. "But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it." In many cases, he added, "humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better."

Amodei said AI companies didn't differ much on automating specific tasks. Some AI CEOs, he wrote, repeated slogans like "human control and agency" and "AI should be just a tool" but still shipped products built for more and more automation.

Anthropic, by contrast, refused to allow its existing models to be used for autonomous weapons during its dispute with the Pentagon. He was "willing to risk Anthropic's future as a company" over that refusal, "even in the face of legal sanctions," Amodei wrote.

title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
excerpt: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
title_en: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
excerpt_en: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
content_en:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
title_en: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
excerpt_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.
content_en:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”

Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing *specific* tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

title: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release
excerpt: Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.
title_en: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release
excerpt_en: Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.
content_en:
Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, has been released from custody, his attorney told CNBC on Wednesday.

The confirmation of Alfozan's release came a day after a federal judge in San Francisco said the defendant would be allowed out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite prosecutors' warnings that he posed a serious flight risk.

Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.

Alfozan was scheduled to be released from detention Wednesday morning at 8 a.m. PT. Shortly before that deadline, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian of the Northern District of California urged the court to maintain Alfozan's detention pending trial, "given the significant risk that the defendant will flee to Saudi Arabia if he is released from custody."

In an order posted on the case docket later Wednesday, Judge Vince Chhabria said the court only learned of the government's last-minute bid to block Alfozan's release after he had already been let out.

The government's motion "is therefore denied as moot," Chhabria's order stated. The judge set a hearing for Dec. 3 on the bid to revoke the magistrate judge's order releasing Alfozan.

Pointing to Alfozan's "ample resources, significant family and professional ties to Saudi Arabia, and few remaining ties to the United States," Missakian had argued in a court filing that the release conditions imposed by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse "are insufficient to safeguard the defendant's appearance for future proceedings in this case."

Alfozan "presents a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate," Missakian wrote.

His office sought to pause the magistrate judge's release order until a ruling on a motion to revoke it. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Alfozan's release.

Tse in a court hearing Tuesday ruled in favor of Rizk's motion for his client's release, which said prosecutors have admitted finding "no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

In a text message to CNBC after that hearing, Rizk said, "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case."

But Missakian's filing Wednesday morning pushed back, saying "the government's investigation of this seven-week-old case is ongoing."

Prosecutors have so far found "hundreds of audio files" on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, at least one of which involved representatives of a foreign government and many of which involved discussions of what may be trade secrets," according to the filing.

"To be sure, what the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation, but the absence of that evidence at this point has no bearing" on whether Alfozan is a flight risk, Missakian argued.

Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.

Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.

*— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report.*

content_en:
# OpenAI wants companies to trust it with sensitive work by promising not to look at their data

**OpenAI is testing a new feature called "Private Inference" that lets companies run queries on its most powerful models without OpenAI being able to access the data.** CEO Sam Altman said the company is now piloting the previously announced offering with its first enterprise customers. Better privacy makes AI useful for a much wider range of work, Altman wrote.

Shekar, the OpenAI employee leading the effort, called it a first step toward "private intelligence for everyone." OpenAI is currently scaling up the compute capacity needed to expand the offering. For now, Private Inference targets business customers, whose data OpenAI already doesn't use for training. Consumer ChatGPT conversations, by contrast, are used for training by default unless users opt out.

With Private Inference, queries are processed on specially isolated hardware whose security can be independently verified, according to OpenAI. Altman also pointed to Private Safety Processing, a system that lets OpenAI scan for abuse without storing customer data. Flagged content is encrypted and stored in the customer's own cloud, and only a secured review system can read it. Google is pursuing a similar approach with Private AI Compute.

content_en:
# Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store.

**Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store.** In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access. Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports. Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year.

Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon. It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity. Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune.

Muse is Meta's most successful consumer AI product so far, with more than 10 million users in the US and Canada. Meta is already seeing gains in its Instagram ad business because Muse helps users organize saved products, which boosts conversion rates for advertisers, CNBC reports. Data from Forter Intelligence shows that Muse recently accounted for 51 percent of all agentic orders, followed by SpaceX's Grok at 24 percent and OpenAI's ChatGPT at 22 percent.

content_en:
Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from *Fortune*. The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue.

# Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block

Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune.

As reported by *Fortune*, Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to *The Verge*’s request for comment.

Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
excerpt: Amazon and Meta are discussing a potential deal that would end a two-month-long blockade of Muse.
title_en: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
excerpt_en: Amazon and Meta are discussing a potential deal that would end a two-month-long blockade of Muse.
content_en:
Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.

According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.

Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.

Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.

Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

content_en:
# US chip-access curbs and anti-distillation measures are reportedly already slowing Chinese AI labs

**The US is tightening its grip in the AI race with China, and the push is already having an effect, according to The Information.** Chinese AI developers including Deepseek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba have been under pressure since September, squeezed by restrictions on Chinese firms' remote access to advanced Nvidia chips in foreign data centers and by successful anti-distillation measures from OpenAI and Anthropic.

As a result, many ongoing projects are facing delays, the report says. Last month, Deepseek researchers internally estimated that their gap to top US models could grow from three to six months to nine months if distillation disappears completely. Moonshot AI has already canceled a $150 million deal for Nvidia Blackwell chips in Indonesia.

Chinese firms are now looking for new workarounds, the publication reports. Some are trying to rent computing power through non-Chinese third parties, while companies such as MiniMax, Mihoyo, and Alibaba are leaning more heavily on domestic chips. They are also investing more in training data for their own reinforcement learning.

title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
title_en: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
content_en:
# Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of *scientific trust*: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

## Helping researchers check the work

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

## Keep scientific judgment in the loop

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's un

title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
excerpt: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.
title_en: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
excerpt_en: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.
content_en:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.

Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.

The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.

While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors.

It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns.

While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them.

“These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”

TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

content_en:
In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

# FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space

SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.

SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.

Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
excerpt: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.
title_en: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
excerpt_en: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.
content_en:
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”

Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)

Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

content_en:
Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.

# Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case

The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations.

Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”

As previously reported by *Bloomberg*, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to *Bloomberg*.

The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it

The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck. ⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. […]
title_en: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
excerpt_en: ⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck. ⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. […]
content_en:
Nvidia has made clear it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck.

Anita Verma-Lallian has been selling exactly that. Her company, Arizona Land Consulting, assembles data center sites for developers, hyperscalers, AI labs, and neoclouds, giving her a view into who’s buying, what makes a site viable, and where projects are running into trouble. She also partners with investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who has been predicting an industry shakeout.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Verma-Lallian about who bears the risk when Nvidia gets pickier, why speculative projects could be the first to fall apart, and what a 2027 shakeout might look like.

Listen to the full episode to hear more about:

- What “land, power, shell” means, and why having all three could give some developers a major advantage.

- How community opposition and state-level restrictions are making some markets harder to build in than others.

- Utilities getting major customers like TSMC to help fund the infrastructure needed to deliver more power.

- Who gets stuck with the bill when a data center project stalls, from developers to lenders to customers.

- Why AI labs and hyperscalers might increasingly build their own data centers instead of relying on neoclouds.

- Who could benefit from a 2027 shakeout, including the companies best positioned to acquire distressed projects.

Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.
